digest.top_line: kV RT over nasal cartilage, 671 BCC/SCC lesions: 5-yr cure 88.09%, 10-yr 86.51%, cosmesis good or acceptable in 96.84%. Retrospective single-institution series.
digest.tldr: Skin RT carried the day. Retrospective nasal/facial BCC/SCC series report 5-yr local control or cure of 85% (orthovoltage), 88.09% (kV) and 89% (HDR mold), all single-institution with physician-rated cosmesis. Brantsch: desmoplasia (LR HR 16.11) and thickness >6.0 mm drive failure after margin-controlled excision without adjuvant RT. Prostate: GnRH antagonist ~37% numerically lower MACE, crude claims comparison.

sites.intro: Real-world claims data on ADT class and MACE; no CI or adjusted HR in source for the antagonist signal.

studies.name: ADT Class and Cardiovascular Risk (Hahn, ASCO GU 2026)
studies.tldr: MACE ~four per 100 person-yrs overall; ~37% numerically lower with GnRH antagonist vs agonist; 11 per 100 person-yrs with preexisting CVD.
details: 🔍 Retrospective real-world claims analysis, commercial + Medicare databases, ~17,000 pts starting ADT
🔍 Index date = first ADT prescription (GnRH agonist or antagonist); data through May 2024
🔍 Primary endpoints: two- and three-point MACE; secondary: MACE pre vs post-2021

subdetails: GnRH agonist (e.g. leuprolide): ~90%
GnRH antagonist: ~10%
Antagonist split: degarelix ~two-thirds, relugolix ~a third

details: 📊 Overall MACE ~four events per 100 person-yrs
📊 Antagonist vs agonist: MACE ~37% numerically lower; no CI or adjusted HR reported in source
📊 Preexisting CVD: ~11 MACE per 100 person-yrs, ~threefold the overall rate
📊 Post-2021 vs pre-2021: modest MACE reduction; no effect size reported in source
⚠️ Agonist pts older, more often Medicare, longer median f/u: crude comparison confounded
⚠️ Antagonist arm mostly degarelix; relugolix uptake after May 2024 not captured
🔗 vs HERO: same direction as relugolix's lower MACE signal, but claims data cannot test it

verdict.rationale: Retrospective claims comparison, 'numerically lower' with no CI or adjustment reported; agonist group older, more Medicare, longer f/u. Antagonist group mostly degarelix.
verdict.audience: Prostate cancer pts starting GnRH agonist or antagonist ADT

studies.monday_clinic: In men with preexisting cardiovascular disease starting ADT, this supports flagging them for cardiology or primary care input given ~11 MACE per 100 person-yrs; it does not establish antagonist superiority over agonist, which rests on an unadjusted, degarelix-dominated comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective real-world analysis of **commercial and Medicare claims databases**, indexed at the date ADT was prescribed. Data cutoff **May 2024**. Presented at ASCO GU 2026 and discussed in a UroToday interview, not a full paper.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **~17,000 pts** with prostate cancer receiving ADT. **~90% GnRH agonist**, **~10% GnRH antagonist** (degarelix ~two-thirds, relugolix ~a third). Agonist pts were older, more likely on Medicare, and had longer median f/u.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** two- and three-point MACE. Secondary: MACE before vs after 2021, the year HERO and PRONOUNCE reported.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall MACE **~four per 100 person-yrs**. Antagonist pts had **~37% numerically lower** MACE than agonist pts. Preexisting CVD carried **~11 per 100 person-yrs**, about threefold. Post-2021 showed a **modest reduction** vs pre-2021.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Direction matches HERO, which the presenter cited for lower MACE with relugolix vs agonist. PRONOUNCE was cited for the value of cardiologist involvement, which frames the preexisting-CVD finding as a referral question, not only a drug-choice question.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents insured US pts starting GnRH agonist or degarelix-dominant antagonist ADT through May 2024. Does not represent current relugolix-heavy practice or a relugolix-specific estimate.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Baseline age, payer and f/u imbalances bias the crude class comparison. MACE misses earlier cardiometabolic harm (diabetes, metabolic syndrome, renal dysfunction), as the interviewer pointed out. The pre/post-2021 shift is a secular trend with no causal link to the trials.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The more robust signal is the preexisting-CVD rate, which identifies who needs cardiovascular co-management whatever the ADT class. A PCF consensus statement on risk-tiered cardiology referral is described as forthcoming.

studies.interpretation:
The headline everyone will take from this analysis is the antagonist-versus-agonist gap, and it is the least defensible number in it. The comparison is crude as described: the presenter calls the reduction "numerically lower" and gives no confidence interval, adjusted hazard ratio or propensity approach, while noting that agonist recipients were older, more often on Medicare and followed for longer. Each of those imbalances pushes the agonist group toward more observed events independent of drug class. Older age raises baseline cardiovascular risk directly. Medicare enrollment tracks age and comorbidity. Longer follow-up, when the outcome is expressed per person-time, should in principle be absorbed by the denominator, but it also places more agonist exposure in earlier calendar years, before the awareness shift the authors themselves describe after 2021. A 37% crude difference produced under those conditions could shrink a great deal once adjusted, and the source gives no way to know.

The antagonist group also is not the drug that generated the original hypothesis. HERO, which the presenter cites as the backdrop, concerned relugolix. Here roughly two-thirds of antagonist exposure was degarelix and only about a third relugolix, and the data stop in May 2024, before the relugolix uptake the presenter acknowledges. The analysis therefore cannot speak to relugolix specifically, and pooling two antagonists with different routes and pharmacology into one class label assumes a class effect that the interviewer explicitly declined to adjudicate. Read honestly, this is consistent with HERO's direction without adding independent evidence for it.

The finding with more practical weight is the preexisting-cardiovascular-disease stratum: about 11 MACE per 100 person-years against roughly four overall. That contrast is less exposed to the confounding that undermines the class comparison, because it describes absolute risk in an identifiable group rather than attributing an effect to a treatment choice. It moves a decision a clinician can act on regardless of which GnRH agent is used: who should have cardiology or primary care involvement when ADT starts. This is where PRONOUNCE enters the argument as the presenter frames it, as evidence that cardiologist involvement matters, and where the forthcoming PCF consensus statement on risk-tiered referral is aimed.

Two further cautions belong with the result. First, MACE is an end-stage composite. The interviewer's point that it misses diabetes, metabolic syndrome, atherosclerosis and renal dysfunction means event rates here understate the cardiometabolic cost of ADT, especially across the multi-year exposure now typical as survival lengthens. Second, the modest post-2021 decline is a calendar-time trend in a claims dataset. Changes in coding, case mix, statin use or general cardiovascular care could produce it as easily as awareness generated by HERO and PRONOUNCE.

For this to change ADT class selection, it would need an adjusted, relugolix-specific estimate with a modern data window and an interval excluding no effect. Until then it supports a narrower claim: men with established cardiovascular disease starting ADT carry roughly threefold MACE risk, and that risk warrants co-management whatever the agent.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: The preexisting-CVD rate of ~11 MACE per 100 person-yrs, about threefold the overall rate, is the actionable signal: it identifies who needs cardiology or primary care co-management at ADT start. The ~37% antagonist advantage is unadjusted and mostly degarelix, so it does not settle relugolix vs agonist choice.

open_questions: Does the antagonist MACE difference persist after adjustment for age and payer?
Does risk-tiered cardiology referral lower MACE on ADT?

sites.intro: Five retrospective single-centre series: four RT series (orthovoltage, kV, two HDR contact techniques) and one surgical cohort that defines high-risk cSCC features.

studies.name: RT for nasal skin SCC, Princess Margaret experience
studies.tldr: Local relapse-free rate 90% at 2y and 85% at 5y, CSS 96%, no RTOG G4 late toxicity in 94 pts treated with mostly orthovoltage RT.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution chart review, 100 pts treated 1982-1993; 6 lost to follow-up, 94 analyzed
🔍 T1 60, T2 11, T4 7, TX 16; only 1 pt node-positive at presentation
🔍 RT alone in 63 pts (67%); surgery then RT in 31 (33%) for gross or microscopic residual

subdetails: <2 cm: 35 Gy in 5 fractions
2-5 cm: 45 Gy in 10 fractions
>5 cm or bone/cartilage invasion: 50 Gy in 20 fractions
Field edge typically 1 cm beyond the gross lesion

details: 🔍 Modality: orthovoltage 76 pts (81%), electrons 13 (14%), cobalt 4 (4%)

details.text: 📊 Actuarial outcomes from start of RT

details: 📊 Elective nodes not irradiated; regional failure in only 2 of 93 cN0 pts
📊 10 local failures: 6 on the nasal bridge, 2 columella (2 of 5 columella lesions failed)
📊 Salvage in 8 pts (4 excision, 4 re-RT); 5 reached disease-free status
⚠️ Late toxicity not formally scored; G4-free claim rests on retrospective chart review
⚠️ Median follow-up only 2.9y in survivors; OS 51% at 5y shrinks the at-risk denominator
⚠️ Univariate analysis found no prognostic factor, likely underpowered with 10 local events
🔗 vs Mazeron series cited in source (1676 nose/vestibule cases): 11% SCC local failure, similar to 10% here at 2y

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series without a surgical comparator; toxicity and cosmesis not formally scored; short survivor follow-up in an elderly cohort.
verdict.audience: Nasal skin SCC (excl. vestibule), mostly T1N0, elderly, primary or postop RT

studies.significance: Failure pattern is the RT read: 6 of 10 local failures sat on the nasal bridge, and 3 of 4 bridge recurrences after CR had a marginal component, while 2 of 5 columella lesions failed. Curved surfaces and fusion planes argue for generous margins beyond the usual 1 cm.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with cN0 nasal skin SCC selected for RT over excision, this supports definitive hypofractionated RT to the primary alone with nodal surveillance; it does not extend to nasal vestibule SCC.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective chart review of **100 pts** treated at Princess Margaret 1982-1993; **94 analyzed** after 6 lost to follow-up. Median follow-up **2.9y** (range 0.2-10.4) in the 45 survivors.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Histologically confirmed SCC of the **nasal skin**; nasal vestibule SCC excluded. T1 60, T2 11, T4 7, TX 16; only 1 pt N1 at presentation.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **35 Gy/5** for lesions <2 cm, **45 Gy/10** for 2-5 cm, **50 Gy/20** for >5 cm or bone/cartilage invasion. Orthovoltage in 81%, energy chosen by lesion thickness (75-100 keV <2 mm, 125 keV 2-4 mm, 250 keV >4 mm); 1-cm field-edge margin; **no elective nodal coverage**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** local failure-free rate. Secondary: nodal failure-free rate, OS, cause-specific survival, late toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No RTOG G4 late toxicity** and no cartilage or bone necrosis. Skin pallor, atrophy and telangiectasia common 1-5y post-RT, progressive but usually asymptomatic.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The Mazeron nose and vestibule series cited by the authors reported **11%** local failure for SCC, in line with the **10%** 2y local failure here. A cited vestibule series reported 5y local relapse-free **80%**, consistent with the authors' point that vestibule disease does worse and was rightly excluded.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with mostly T1N0 nasal skin SCC treated with definitive or postoperative RT. Does not represent nasal vestibule SCC or clinically node-positive disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Treatment-era orthovoltage technique and no formal cosmetic assessment, so the **optimal schedule cannot be derived**. Dose was chosen by size and frailty, confounding any dose-response read.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors now prefer **50 Gy/20** or **60 Gy/30** for large infiltrative lesions, since schedules under 4 weeks usually leave a visible cosmetic defect after 1-2y. Many elderly pts still accept 1-2 week courses and the cosmetic trade-off.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series is less the headline control rate than the failure map. A local failure-free rate of 90% at 2 years sits comfortably beside the 11% SCC local failure figure from the Mazeron experience the authors cite, so the result does not move the established view that RT is an effective definitive option for nasal skin SCC. What it adds is where control is lost. Six of ten local failures were on the bridge, and three of four bridge recurrences after a complete response had a marginal component, while two of five columella lesions failed. The authors read this as underestimation of tumor extent on curved surfaces and along embryonic fusion planes, a plausible mechanism that argues for generous margins and careful attention to dose fall-off where source-to-surface distance changes over the nasal contour.

The nodal finding is the second actionable point. Apart from one patient, nobody received intentional nodal coverage, and only 2 of 93 clinically node-negative patients failed regionally, with no adverse primary feature predicting it. That supports surveillance rather than elective nodal RT for cN0 disease, with the caveat that small numbers and short follow-up limit how much reassurance an absence of events can provide.

Confidence should be tempered in three directions. First, this is a retrospective chart review in which dose was chosen by lesion size, depth and patient frailty, so any attempt to infer dose-response is confounded by indication; the null univariate analysis with ten local events says more about power than biology. Second, the toxicity claim is weaker than the abstract suggests: late effects were not formally scored, so the absence of G4 events means none were documented, not that they were systematically sought, and cosmesis by schedule could not be assessed. Third, median follow-up in survivors was 2.9 years, and with 5-year OS of 51% in an elderly cohort, competing mortality thins the population in whom late local failure or late cartilage toxicity could surface. The 96% cause-specific survival largely reflects that patients die of other causes.

The treatment era also matters for transfer. Most patients were treated with orthovoltage selected by lesion thickness, a technique still in use but now often replaced by electrons with bolus or brachytherapy molds, which carry different surface and depth dosimetry on the nose. The authors' own shift toward 50 Gy in 20 fractions, or 60 Gy in 30 for large infiltrative lesions, is driven by cosmesis rather than control, and their observation that elderly patients often accept a 1-2 week course with a cosmetic penalty frames the real decision: schedule length against appearance, not against local control.

The series would be wrong to lean on if bridge and columella failures reflected selection of larger or neglected tumors rather than geometry, or if longer follow-up revealed late chondritis that chart review missed. It leaves untouched the comparison with Mohs excision, which this cohort, already selected for RT in a multidisciplinary setting, cannot address.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Bridge and columella lesions drove local failure: 6 of 10 failures were on the bridge, 3 of 4 post-CR bridge recurrences had a marginal component, and 2 of 5 columella lesions failed. Margin and contour dosimetry, not dose, look like the lever, with no elective nodal coverage needed in cN0.

open_questions: Optimal dose-fractionation balancing cosmesis and local control
Electrons or brachytherapy vs orthovoltage on curved nasal surfaces
RT vs Mohs excision for nasal skin SCC

studies.name: Risk factors determining prognosis of cutaneous SCC (Brantsch)
studies.tldr: No metastases in tumours ≤2.0 mm thick; >6.0 mm metastasized in 14/90 (16%); desmoplasia drove local recurrence (HR 16.11) after margin-controlled resection.
details: 🔍 Prospective single-centre cohort (Tübingen), resections 1990-2001; 653 enrolled, 615 assessable
🔍 Median f/u 43 mo (range 1-165); median age 73; 38 lost to follow-up
🔍 All resected with 3D-histology to tumour-free margins; no pt received adjuvant RT

details.text: 📐 Best multivariate Cox model, independent factors

details: 📊 Local recurrence 12/51 (24%) desmoplastic vs 8/564 (1%) non-desmoplastic
🔍 Perineural or perivascular invasion was always coded as desmoplasia, so the desmoplasia HR includes PNI

details.text: 📐 Predictive accuracy (C-index), best model vs current TNM
subdetails: Metastasis: 0.837 vs 0.743
Local recurrence: 0.907 vs 0.750

details: 📊 First metastasis always in a regional LN; none after year 4, no LR after year 6
⚠️ Events per predictor 26:7 (metastasis) and 20:7 (LR), below the limit of 5 the authors cite
⚠️ Lip location and poor differentiation (both TNM-era criteria) were not independent prognostic factors

verdict.rationale: Single-centre prognostic cohort, model selected by forward selection with events per predictor below 5. Validated only internally; no external cohort.
verdict.audience: Primary cutaneous SCC, resected to clear 3D-histology margins, no adjuvant RT

studies.significance: Desmoplasia, which here included every case of perineural or perivascular invasion, carried local recurrence of 12/51 (24%) vs 8/564 (1%) despite tumour-free 3D-histology margins and no adjuvant RT. That is an RT-naive surgical baseline. It places the adjuvant RT question in desmoplastic/PNI or >6.0 mm tumours (LR 11/90, 12%), not in clear-margin thin SCC.
studies.monday_clinic: In resected cSCC with clear margins that is ≤2.0 mm thick and non-desmoplastic, this supports a very low expectation of metastasis or recurrence. It does not address whether adjuvant RT changes risk in desmoplastic or >6.0 mm tumours, because no pt received RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective single-centre observational cohort following **STROBE**. Pts were resected between 1990 and 2001, follow-up closed Dec 2005, **median f/u 43 mo**. Cox models used forward selection, with a 200/415 learning-validation split for **internal validation only**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **615 assessable white pts** with primary cutaneous SCC at any body site, median age 73, 5% immunosuppressed. Excluded: SCC in situ, keratoacanthoma, collision tumours, and recurrent SCC treated elsewhere.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **No pt received adjuvant RT.** Every resection reached tumour-free margins by 3D-histology, with re-excision as needed, so outcomes reflect surgery alone.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: The source states the **primary endpoints** as time to metastasis and time to local recurrence, each measured from diagnosis of the primary. Seven candidate predictors were chosen a priori.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 26 (4%) metastases and 20 (3%) local recurrences. **No tumour ≤2.0 mm metastasized**. The thinnest tumour that metastasized was 2.8 mm thick.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Clayman and colleagues reported LR in **12% (15 of 130)** of primary SCC. Margin-controlled resection here gave **3% (20 of 615)**. The authors cite an Australian series of 266 pts with nodal disease that also supports tumour thickness over horizontal size.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents white pts with primary cutaneous SCC resected to tumour-free 3D-histology margins without adjuvant RT. Does not represent SCC in situ, keratoacanthoma, recurrent SCC treated elsewhere, or pts managed with adjuvant RT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Follow-up after the early period relied partly on mailed questionnaires to treating physicians. **New field-cancerization SCC can mimic local recurrence**. University referral may have enriched for poorly differentiated tumours.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Thickness, immunosuppression and desmoplasia outperformed **Broders' grade and horizontal size** as prognostic factors. The authors propose thickness-based T1-T3 cutoffs (≤2.0, 2.1-6.0, >6.0 mm) with "d" and "i" modifiers. The study does not test whether any treatment changes the high-risk course.

studies.interpretation:
This cohort is one of the main sources behind the idea that depth, rather than diameter or grade, organises risk in cutaneous SCC. Its strongest result is the simplest one. In 207 tumours ≤2.0 mm thick there were no metastases, and only one local recurrence. A negative stratum that clean, in an unselected referral population followed for a median of 43 months, is harder to explain away than any of the hazard ratios. It is also the result least affected by the model-building problems below, because it is a raw count rather than a fitted estimate. Since metastases clustered in the first year and none appeared after year 4, the follow-up was long enough for this stratum.

The multivariate models deserve less confidence than their p-values suggest. With 26 metastases and 20 local recurrences against seven candidate predictors, the events-per-variable ratio is below the threshold the authors themselves cite. Forward selection in that setting tends to overfit and to inflate the size of the effects it keeps. The desmoplasia HR of 16.11 for local recurrence, with an interval running from 6.57 to 39.49, should be read as showing a large direction of effect rather than a precise magnitude. The learning-validation split helps a little, but the two samples come from the same centre, the same pathologists and the same surgical technique. In the learning sample, the second factor selected for metastasis was poor differentiation, which then failed in the validation sample. That instability is the warning.

For a radiation oncologist, this is a natural-history cohort, not an RT study. Every pt was resected to tumour-free margins under 3D-histology, and nobody received adjuvant RT. So the 24% local recurrence in desmoplastic tumours is a recurrence rate after clear margins with no adjuvant treatment. That matters because desmoplasia here was defined to include every case of perineural or perivascular invasion, the same histology that commonly prompts discussion of post-op RT. The cohort identifies where adjuvant RT is worth considering. It cannot say whether RT closes that gap, and nothing in it informs dose, volume or elective nodal coverage. The finding that the first metastasis was always a regional node supports the authors' focus on nodal staging and ultrasound surveillance. That pattern is also the clinical basis for thinking about the regional basin in high-risk pts.

The main limit on generalising is the surgery. Margin-controlled excision with re-excision to clearance likely explains why overall local recurrence was 3%, against the 12% Clayman and colleagues reported. A practice using conventional excision with standard margin assessment should expect higher baseline recurrence, so these strata may understate the absolute risk elsewhere. The cohort was also entirely white and mostly immunocompetent. With only 31 immunosuppressed pts, the immunosuppression HR rests on a handful of events and says little about transplant recipients.

The result would be wrong in its details if an external cohort with adequate events found the 6.0 mm cutoff drifting or the desmoplasia effect shrinking a long way. The ≤2.0 mm no-risk stratum is the part most likely to hold.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Desmoplasia, which included all PNI, carried LR of 12/51 (24%) vs 8/564 (1%) after clear margins with no adjuvant RT. This RT-naive baseline sets where adjuvant RT is worth weighing: desmoplastic/PNI or >6.0 mm tumours. The cohort cannot show that RT lowers that risk.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Clear 3D-histology margins with 2-10 mm safety margins held overall LR to 20 of 615 (3%), yet desmoplastic tumours still recurred locally in 24%. The first metastatic site was always a regional LN, which is why the authors raise SLNB and nodal ultrasound for high-risk pts.

open_questions: Does adjuvant RT reduce LR in desmoplastic/PNI or >6.0 mm cSCC?
Role of SLNB in high-risk cSCC
External validation of thickness cutoffs in larger cohorts

studies.name: Kilovoltage RT for carcinomas overlying nasal cartilage (671 lesions)
studies.tldr: 5-yr cure rate 88.09% and 10-yr 86.51% in 671 BCC and SCC over nasal cartilage; cosmesis good or acceptable in 96.84%.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution series, 671 basal and squamous cell carcinomas, treated 1972-2007
🔍 Mean f/u 38.016 mo (range 1-351 mo); actuarial cure rate by life-table method

subdetails: 55-60 kV, 4-6 mA, no filter, HVD 2-12 mm
5 Gy/fx, 2 times per week
Total 30-75 Gy (mean 55.70 Gy, median 55 Gy)
Field margin 0.5-1 cm; 1.5 cm for 20 morpheaform BCC
Nostril lead rubber shield (1 mm Pb) for alae nasi lesions
HDRT + CRT in 3 lesions only (50 + 15 Gy or 60 + 20/25 Gy)

details: 📊 Recurrence onset 3-96 mo (mean 37.96 mo); 37 of 38 relapses BCC
📊 No relapse association with dose or lesion size
📊 Authors report 0 complications or sequelae
⚠️ Crude 5.66% recurrence understates failure; actuarial 5-yr cure 88.09% is the real figure
⚠️ Toxicity is clinician-rated cosmesis; no cartilage-necrosis grading scale stated
⚠️ Superiority over other modalities rests on cross-literature comparison only, with no surgical arm
🔗 Authors cite randomised facial BCC data favouring surgery overall, with cosmesis similar on nasal skin

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective series, 1972-2007, no surgical comparator; the authors' claim of superiority over other modalities rests on cross-literature comparison this design cannot support.
verdict.audience: BCC and SCC of skin overlying nasal cartilage

studies.significance: Failure was mostly marginal (25 of 38 recurrences) with 0.5-1 cm field margins, which argues for generous margins over nasal skin; morpheaform lesions got 1.5 cm. With 5 Gy twice weekly (median 55 Gy), the authors report no cartilage sequelae. That supports kV RT as the nonsurgical option where excision would need complex reconstruction.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with BCC or SCC of skin over the nasal cartilage whose excision would need complex reconstruction, this supports superficial kV RT as a durable nonsurgical option; with no surgical arm, it does not settle RT vs excision for a surgically straightforward lesion.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective single-institution series of **671 lesions** treated 1972-2007. Mean follow-up **38.016 mo** (range 1-351). Actuarial cure rate by life-table method; chi-squared for dose and size associations.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Basal and squamous cell carcinomas** of the skin overlying the nasal cartilages. Histology split of the full cohort not given in the source excerpt. Relapses included 10 lesions already recurrent after prior non-radiological treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: CRT in 668 lesions: **55-60 kV**, HVD 2-12 mm, **5 Gy/fx twice weekly**, total 30-75 Gy (median **55 Gy**). Margin **0.5-1 cm**, 1.5 cm for morpheaform BCC. Septal cartilage shielded with 1 mm Pb nostril inserts at the alae.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: CR **98.80%** at 1 mo; **5-yr cure 88.09%**, **10-yr 86.51%**. Recurrence 38 lesions (13 central, **25 marginal**), onset 3-96 mo. No relationship between relapse and dose or size.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Cosmesis good or acceptable in **96.84%**; 16 lesions not acceptable. Authors report **no complications or sequelae**, and flag the 7 newly not-acceptable cases for continued follow-up.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: No contemporaneous comparator. The authors cite randomised facial BCC data comparing RT with surgery: cosmesis was similar on nasal skin but control favoured surgery, in tumors under 4 cm treated with mixed RT techniques. Mohs surgery, the usual comparator for nasal BCC today, is not addressed.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCC and SCC of the skin over the nasal cartilages treated mainly with superficial kV RT (668 of 671 lesions). Does not represent pts treated with higher-energy or interstitial techniques, used in only 3 lesions here.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Toxicity is clinician-rated cosmesis without a named scale, and a mean follow-up near 3 years is short for late cartilage effects. The null dose-relapse finding is likely confounded by dose being chosen by lesion size.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The data support kV RT as an effective, cartilage-sparing option for nasal skin carcinoma, where tight adherence of skin to cartilage complicates excision. They do not establish superiority over surgery, and the marginal-failure pattern raises the question of whether margins were adequate.

studies.interpretation:
The headline that matters is the actuarial one. A crude recurrence rate of 5.66% sits beside a 5-year cure rate of 88.09%, and the gap is the follow-up: a mean of about 38 months, with some lesions seen for as little as one month, while recurrences surfaced anywhere from 3 to 96 months after treatment. Read the crude figure and kV RT looks near-perfect. Read the life-table figure, plus a 10-year rate of 86.51%, and it looks like good, durable control with most failures arriving in the first several years. The actuarial number is the one to quote to a colleague or a tumor board.

The pattern of failure is more useful to a radiation oncologist than the cure rate. Twenty-five of 38 recurrences were marginal, not central. That is a geometry problem rather than a dose problem, which matches the authors' finding of no association between relapse and dose. Margins of 0.5-1 cm over the nose are tight by many current superficial-RT conventions, and the authors already widened to 1.5 cm for morpheaform BCC because its edge is hard to define clinically. A reasonable reading is that the infiltrative-edge problem was not limited to the lesions labelled morpheaform. The null dose-response should not be over-read. Dose was almost certainly chosen by lesion size and depth, so the analysis cannot separate the two, and with 38 events the comparison has little power.

The toxicity claim needs the most caution. The paper reports no complications or sequelae over a span that includes 5 Gy fractions delivered over nasal cartilage, which is exactly the setting where large fractions raise concern for chondritis and necrosis. That is reassuring, but the ascertainment is a clinician's cosmetic grade without a named scale, follow-up is short relative to late cartilage effects, and the authors themselves flag 7 not-acceptable cosmetic results that need ongoing review. Absence of reported necrosis in a retrospective chart series is weaker evidence than absence in a prospectively graded cohort.

The authors' conclusion, that dermatologic RT is superior to any other modality for these lesions, does not follow from a single-arm series compared against literature values with different selection, staging and follow-up. Their own cited randomised data on facial BCC favoured surgery for control while showing similar cosmesis on nasal skin, and that trial predates the routine use of Mohs surgery, which is what most nasal BCC now receives. The series also spans 35 years and mixes BCC with SCC without reporting histology-specific control in the excerpt, so the SCC result is effectively unknown.

Where this lands: it is a large, long-horizon dataset supporting superficial kV RT as a legitimate curative option over the nasal cartilages, particularly for elderly pts or lesions whose excision would need complex reconstruction. It does not move the default for a surgically straightforward lesion in a fit pt, and its main practical lesson for the RT reader is to treat the margin generously.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Failure was mostly marginal (25 of 38 recurrences) with 0.5-1 cm margins, which argues for wider fields over nasal skin. With 5 Gy twice weekly (median 55 Gy), the authors report no cartilage sequelae, supporting kV RT where excision would need complex reconstruction.

open_questions: Local control vs Mohs surgery for nasal skin carcinoma
Adequate field margin given mostly marginal recurrences
Late cartilage toxicity of 5 Gy fractions beyond 10 years

studies.name: Facial cutaneous carcinoma HDR contact brachytherapy with customized molds
studies.tldr: 5-yr actuarial LC 89% (100% flat surfaces, 83% nose) with Ir-192 HDR contact mold BT, 48 Gy/12 fx, for facial BCC/SCC ≤3 mm thick.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution series (FIVO Valencia), 51 lesions in 48 pts, treated 1999-2005
🔍 BCC 42 (82.4%), SCC 9 (17.6%); mean diameter 1.5 cm (range 0.5-4 cm); all ≤3 mm thick
🔍 Median age 78; radical intent 95%, adjuvant 5% (lateral margin involved after incomplete surgery)

details.text: 💊 HDR schedules used (Ir-192, every other day, 3 fx/wk)

rows: 35 Gy, 7 Gy x 5 fx (very old pts)

details: 🔍 Prescription at 3 mm depth; 1 cm margin on lesion; skin surface dose ~150%, never higher
🔍 Nose: custom 5 mm wax mold on plaster cast, CT-planned; flat sites: 5 mm bolus with tubes 1 cm apart
📊 Local control by site (median f/u 45 mo, range 4-102)
📊 All 5 relapses treated with only three tubes; 2 at field border, 3 in-field
📊 All relapses salvaged with surgery; no nodal or distant spread; no cancer deaths

subdetails: Acute G1-2 dermatitis: 30 pts (78%), resolved in days
Acute G4 dermatitis: 11 pts (21%), healed in 3 wk as outpatient
No late complications reported, including nasal chondritis
Some G1 hypopigmentation, G2 telangiectasia, mainly large tumors
Cosmesis good or very good in all cases

details: ⚠️ G4 dermatitis rate inconsistent within paper: 21% in Results, 12% in Discussion
⚠️ Cosmesis graded on a physician scale (poor to very good), no validated pt-reported instrument
🔗 vs Guix et al. (contact HDR-BT, 60-65 Gy at 1.8 Gy/fx, 136 lesions): 5-yr LC 98% per source

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-arm series, 51 lesions, one institution; no comparator vs Mohs, electrons or orthovoltage. Nasal-tip failures tied to an early three-tube applicator.
verdict.audience: Facial BCC/SCC ≤3 mm thick, ≤4 cm, mostly elderly, non-surgical

studies.significance: Failure tracked the applicator, not the dose: all five relapses had only three catheters, and four sat on the nasal tip (LC 73%) versus 95% on pyramid/wing and 100% on flat skin. The 3 mm prescription depth only fits lesions ≤3 mm, so nasal-tip lesions or thicker tumors argue for electrons, interstitial BT or surgery.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly pt with a thin (≤3 mm) facial BCC/SCC on the temple, forehead, cheek or nasal dorsum/ala, this supports HDR contact mold BT as a surgical alternative; it does not extend to nasal-tip lesions or tumors thicker than 3 mm.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution series, 51 lesions in 48 pts referred 1999-2005. **Median follow-up 45 mo** (range 4-102); LC by Kaplan-Meier.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Facial BCC (82.4%) and SCC (17.6%), mean diameter 1.5 cm (0.5-4 cm), **thickness ≤3 mm** in all; thicker lesions went to electrons. Median age 78; 95% radical, 5% adjuvant after lateral-margin-positive excision.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Ir-192 HDR contact BT via custom wax nasal molds (CT-planned) or bolus applicators on flat skin, 1 cm margin, **prescribed at 3 mm depth**. Standard **48 Gy in 12 fx of 4 Gy**, 3 fx/wk, over 4 wk; 3 Gy x 17-18 and 7 Gy x 5 schedules also used.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 5 relapses (**9.8%**) at 6-32 mo, all on the nose and all with three-tube applicators. **Nasal tip LC 73%** vs 95% on pyramid/wing; all salvaged surgically.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute G4 dermatitis in **11 pts (21%)**, healed within 3 wk; no late complications including chondritis. Cosmesis good or very good in all cases.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Source cites Guix et al. contact HDR-BT with 5-yr LC 98% at 60-65 Gy/1.8 Gy fx, and Rio et al. LDR interstitial BT with 92.5% radical LC. This series sits below those on the nose, driven by the tip.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents thin (≤3 mm), ≤4 cm facial BCC/SCC on flat skin or nasal dorsum/ala, largely in elderly pts. Does not represent nasal-tip lesions, tumors thicker than 3 mm, or high-risk SCC.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Only 9 SCC, so no histology-specific read. Cosmesis was physician-graded and the G4 dermatitis rate differs between Results (21%) and Discussion (12%).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Authors attribute nasal-tip failure to undersized three-tube molds and poor catheter bending at the tip's lower surface, and now add catheters. A **deeper prescription point** was not excluded as a cause.

studies.interpretation:
The useful content of this series is less the headline 89% five-year control than the pattern of where and why it failed. Every relapse occurred on the nose, every relapse had been treated with the earliest three-catheter version of the wax mold, and four of the five sat on the nasal tip. Two of the five were marginal. That clustering points to a geometric problem, coverage of a highly curved surface by parallel tubes that do not bend enough, rather than an inadequate dose. The two border failures had received 54 and 57 Gy, the upper end of the schedules used, which is hard to reconcile with underdosing as the explanation. A reader planning surface mold work should take the applicator lesson more seriously than the fractionation lesson.

Against the comparators the authors themselves tabulate, the flat-surface result (16 of 16 controlled) is in line with what contact HDR series report, and the Guix experience at 60-65 Gy in 1.8 Gy fractions reached 98% at five years. The nose is where this series falls short of that benchmark, and the gap is almost entirely the tip. Excluding the tip, non-tip nasal control of 95% looks comparable to what electrons or orthovoltage would be expected to deliver, though the series offers no internal comparison and the numbers are small enough that one additional failure shifts the estimate visibly.

Several design features should temper confidence. This is a retrospective series of 51 lesions from one institution, selected for HDR because of size and location, with thickness capped at 3 mm and thicker lesions diverted to electrons. That selection removes exactly the tumors most likely to fail a 3 mm prescription, so the control rate describes a favorable subset. SCC accounts for nine lesions, too few to say anything about histology. Cosmesis was graded on a four-point physician scale with no patient-reported measure. The paper also reports the severe acute dermatitis rate inconsistently, 21% in Results and 12% in the Discussion, which matters because grade 4 skin reaction in roughly a fifth of an elderly cohort is not a trivial trade for a 48 Gy course.

What the series does settle is practical: a 4 Gy by 12 fraction contact HDR course, delivered in short outpatient sessions without anesthesia, is feasible and controls thin lesions on flat facial skin and the nasal dorsum and ala, with surgery available as salvage. What it does not settle is whether the newer multi-catheter molds fix the tip problem, whether a deeper prescription point would have, or how HDR contact BT compares head to head with Mohs or electrons for cosmesis and control. For the tip specifically, the authors' own conclusion is to use another technique, and the data support that reading.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Failure tracked the applicator, not the dose: all five relapses had only three catheters, and four sat on the nasal tip (LC 73%) versus 95% on pyramid/wing and 100% on flat skin. The 3 mm prescription depth only fits lesions ≤3 mm, so nasal-tip lesions or thicker tumors argue for electrons, interstitial BT or surgery.

open_questions: Do multi-catheter nasal molds restore control on the nasal tip?
Contact HDR-BT vs Mohs or electrons for cosmesis and control
Would a deeper prescription point reduce marginal failures?

studies.name: Hypofractionated HDR plesiotherapy in nonmelanoma skin cancer
studies.tldr: 3y/5y DFS 95.12%/93.36% after 3 Gy/fx HDR surface brachy for 134 BCC/SCC lesions; CR 98%, recurrent lesions did worse.
details: 🔍 Retrospective single-institution series: 114 pts, 134 lesions (92 BCC, 42 SCC), Nov 2006 to Dec 2011
🔍 All lesions clinically N0; median f/u 33 mo

subdetails: Definitive: 75 BCC + 27 SCC (77.3%)
Adjuvant after excision with positive/close margins: 32 lesions (22.7%)
Leipzig applicator (2 or 3 cm), ≤2 cm flat lesions: 101 lesions (75.4%)
Customized wax/plaster mold, raised areas or >2 cm lesions
Molds treated larger lesions: mean 19.38 vs 13.07 mm, p=0.004
Ir-192 HDR, 3 Gy/fx, 3 fx/wk
Mean dose 48.79 Gy (45-54) BCC, 50.55 Gy (45-57) SCC
Dose prescribed 3-5 mm below skin surface
PTV: lesion + 0.5-1 cm margin
Lower doses for BCC and adjuvant setting than SCC and definitive

details: 📐 Primary vs recurrent DFS p=0.003; definitive vs adjuvant 94.86% vs 96.3%, p=0.412
📊 CR 98%; 2 persistent lesions, both Leipzig; no regional or distant mets

subdetails: Definitive > adjuvant: OR 2.928 (95% CI 1.287-6.659), p=0.013

details: 📊 Late G0-1 95.2%; one G4 ulcer (recurrent 40 mm lower-leg SCC, venous insufficiency, 54 Gy)
📊 Cosmesis excellent/good 82%, fair 13%, not available 5%
⚠️ Applicator comparison confounded by lesion size and site; not randomized
⚠️ Internal inconsistencies: "six" recurrences listed as five Leipzig + three mold; abstract acute toxicity 57.3% vs 57.5% in results
⚠️ Median f/u 33 mo is short for NMSC late recurrence and late cosmesis

verdict.rationale: Retrospective single-institution series, no comparator arm; applicator comparison confounded by lesion size and location; DFS per lesion with 33-mo median f/u.
verdict.audience: Clinically N0 BCC/SCC skin, primary or recurrent, definitive or adjuvant

studies.significance: Disease status, not applicator, split control: recurrent lesions reached 3y/5y DFS 85.9%/85.9% vs 97.9%/95.6% for primary (p=0.003). Acute G3 was 40.3% at 3 Gy/fx three times weekly, higher with definitive intent and molds, so fraction size and applicator choice gate tolerability more than control for larger or curved lesions.
studies.monday_clinic: In older pts with a small flat primary BCC or SCC, this supports HDR surface brachy at 3 Gy/fx as a definitive option with high control; it is weaker support for recurrent lesions, where 5y DFS was 85.9%.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** single-institution series, 114 pts and **134 lesions** treated Nov 2006 to Dec 2011. Analysis per lesion; median follow-up **33 mo**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 92 BCC and 42 SCC, all **clinically N0**. 77.3% definitive, 22.7% **adjuvant** after excision with positive or close margins.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Ir-192 HDR plesiotherapy, **3 Gy/fx, 3 fx/wk**; mean 48.79 Gy (45-54) for BCC and 50.55 Gy (45-57) for SCC, prescribed 3-5 mm below the surface with a 0.5-1 cm margin. **Leipzig** 2 or 3 cm applicators for flat lesions ≤2 cm (75.4%); **customized molds** for raised or larger lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall 3y/5y DFS **95.12%/93.36%**, CR 98%. Recurrent lesions did worse than primary (**85.9% vs 95.6%** at 5y, p=0.003); applicator and definitive vs adjuvant did not separate DFS.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute RTOG G3 **40.3%**, G4 2.2%; toxicity higher with definitive intent (OR 2.928, p=0.013) and borderline with molds (p=0.067). Late G0-1 95.2%; cosmesis excellent/good **82%**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Authors place results alongside the Kohler Leipzig series (91% complete remission) and Guix's mold series (5y DFS 98%). They cite one randomized surgery vs RT trial as the only head-to-head data, with no numbers given in source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents clinically N0 BCC/SCC treated definitively or adjuvantly with surface HDR. Does not represent nodal disease, deep-invading tumors beyond a 3-5 mm prescription depth, or melanoma.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Molds treated **larger** lesions, so mold vs Leipzig DFS and toxicity differences cannot be separated from size. Reported recurrence counts do not add up, and the acute toxicity figure differs between abstract and results.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Supports surface HDR as a **definitive alternative** to excision for small primary NMSC. It does not settle optimal fraction size, and the high acute G3 rate argues for weighing applicator and dose per fraction for larger lesions.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this series is less the headline DFS than how it is distributed. A 5-year DFS of 93.36% across a mixed cohort of BCC and SCC, primary and recurrent, definitive and adjuvant, sits in the range most single-institution brachytherapy reports describe, and the authors place it alongside the Leipzig experience reported by Kohler and the mold technique reported by Guix. That is reassuring but not discriminating; nearly every retrospective NMSC RT series reports control in the 90s, because lesion selection does much of the work. The more useful signal is that recurrent disease separated clearly from primary (5-year DFS 85.9% vs 95.6%, p=0.003), while applicator type and definitive versus adjuvant intent did not separate meaningfully. For a radiation oncologist, that points to disease history, rather than device, as the variable worth weighing when offering surface brachytherapy as an alternative to re-excision or Mohs.

The applicator comparison is where a reader should be most cautious. Molds were used for larger lesions (mean 19.38 vs 13.07 mm) and for raised or curved surfaces, so any difference in DFS or toxicity between molds and Leipzig cones is confounded by size and anatomy. The authors attempted to address this by restricting to lesions within the Leipzig range, but the toxicity association with molds stayed borderline (p=0.067), and lesion size itself carried a significant odds ratio for acute toxicity. The 5-year DFS of 88% for molds versus 94.9% for Leipzig is better read as a size and site gradient than as evidence that one device controls disease less well. Compounding this, the paper's own accounting is not internally consistent: six recurrences are described as five Leipzig plus three mold, and the acute toxicity figure in the abstract does not match the results section. These are small errors, but in a series this size they are the kind that make subgroup p-values fragile.

The acute toxicity profile deserves more attention than the conclusion gives it. Roughly two in five lesions developed RTOG grade 3 acute reactions at 3 Gy per fraction three times weekly, and definitive treatment carried higher odds than adjuvant. Late outcomes were favourable, with grade 0-1 late toxicity in 95.2% and good or excellent cosmesis in 82%, which is the trade a surface brachytherapy patient is accepting: a brisk acute reaction that largely resolves. Follow-up of 33 months, though, is short for both late cosmesis and late BCC recurrence, so the late picture is incomplete.

What would make this wrong? If the high control reflects selection of small, favourable primaries, the result does not transfer to the recurrent or larger lesions where an RT alternative to surgery is most often requested, and the data in hand already hint that this is the case. The series supports HDR plesiotherapy as a reasonable definitive option for small primary NMSC in older pts, and gives a concrete reason to counsel recurrent-lesion pts on a lower control expectation. It does not establish a preferred fractionation, does not compare against excision or Mohs, and does not show that molds are inferior once size is accounted for.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Disease status, not applicator, split control: recurrent lesions reached 5y DFS 85.9% vs 95.6% for primary (p=0.003). Acute G3 was 40.3% at 3 Gy/fx three times weekly, higher with definitive intent and molds, so fraction size and applicator choice gate tolerability for larger or curved lesions.

open_questions: Optimal fraction size for HDR surface brachy in NMSC
Late recurrence and cosmesis beyond 5 years
HDR plesiotherapy vs Mohs or excision head-to-head
